newsitem.title: JAPAN: Yen/A$ dual bond issuing boom to slow - experts.
newsitem.headline: Yen/A$ dual bond issuing boom to slow - experts.

text.p: The issuing boom in yen/Australian dollar dual currency bonds is likely to slow down rapidly because of Wednesday's surprising credit easing by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), experts and underwriters said.

Overseas issuers, who have been feeding the appetite of Japanese retail investors with such bonds, particularly dual currency samurai bonds, may have to move into other currencies as they may not be able to offer the higher coupon on the yen/Aussie they were extending before the rate cut, they said.

"Considering the currency risks, it will be very difficult to attract Japanese investors if (the dual samurai) bonds don't carry a coupon of more than five percent," said Masaru Hamazaki, deputy manager at Yamaichi Research Institute (YRI).
The RBA announced a cut in the official cash rate by 0.5 point to 6.0 percent on Wednesday morning.

That means foreign fund-raisers may not be able to offer a coupon of more than five percent for yen/Aussie samurais with maturities of about two to three years, the type most popular with private investors, analysts said.
On December 3, U.S. brewer Anheuser-Busch Cos Inc was the last borrower to launch a yen/Aussie dual currency samurai. The two-year bond carried a coupon of 5.1 percent.

The appetite for dual-currency bond buying this year has been extremely strong. Of an estimated 2.1 trillion yen ($18.5 billion) of dual-currency bonds issued in Japan from January to the end of November, around 80 to 90 percent were in yen/Australian dollars, underwriting sources said.
Underwriters, however, said there were already signs issuers were issuing more in U.S. dollars as the interest-rate gap between the United States and Australia had been narrowing.

Even though many yen/U.S. dollar dual samurai issues with durations of two to three years have been launched with coupons below five percent in recent months, investors still wanted to buy them due to the status of the U.S. dollar.
Also, private investors prefer to buy yen/U.S. dollar bonds if the interest rate gap is narrower because the U.S. currency is not as volatile versus the yen as the Australian currency.

"As Australian interest rates have been falling (in recent months), the market's trend was already changing," said Mikio Sugihara, chief manager of the global capital market group at Nomura Securities. "Fund-raisers' focus was shifting more to other currencies, such as the U.S. dollar and the Kiwi.
"I don't expect to see dramatic change in the overall trend, but issues in U.S. dollars are likely to increase," he said.

Underwriters said overseas fund raisers may diversify to other currencies with higher interest rates, possibly to sterling, or they may consider issuing dual currency issues with longer durations in order to provide a higher coupon rate.

"To offer a higher coupon, borrowers have to think about launching dual currency issues with longer durations of about five to seven years," NRI's Hamazaki said. "But I don't know whether retail investors prefer holding such issues."

Some underwriters said dual currency issues, targetting private investors in the winter bonus season, may shrink a bit in the coming months as several domestic brokerage houses rushed to issue them before the end of the year
"We may see the volume of issues falling as several brokerage houses brought forward ones which they had been planning for January and February," a senior underwriter said.
